claim: RUNX1 marks a specific subpopulation of proximal luminal cells (PLCs) enriched in the periurethral region of the developing and adult mouse prostate.
source: Here, we report that the transcription factor RUNX1 marks a specific subpopulation of proximal luminal cells (PLCs), enriched in the periurethral region of the developing and adult mouse prostate, and distinct from the previously identified NKX3.1+ luminal castration-resistant cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B, as well as flow cytometry analysis in Figure 1C,D.

claim: RUNX1+ PLCs are distinct from the previously identified NKX3.1+ luminal castration-resistant cells.
source: Here, we report that the transcription factor RUNX1 marks a specific subpopulation of proximal luminal cells (PLCs), enriched in the periurethral region of the developing and adult mouse prostate, and distinct from the previously identified NKX3.1+ luminal castration-resistant cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative image-based cytometry (QBIC) showing mutually exclusive expression patterns of RUNX1 and NKX3.1 (Figure 1A,B).

claim: RUNX1+ PLCs are unaffected by androgen deprivation.
source: Using scRNA-seq profiling and genetic lineage tracing, we show that RUNX1+ PLCs are unaffected by androgen deprivation, and do not contribute to the regeneration of the distal luminal compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing experiments showing stable absolute numbers of RFP+ cells after castration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D) and increased frequency in the epithelial compartment (Figure 4E).

claim: RUNX1+ PLCs do not contribute to the regeneration of the distal luminal compartments.
source: Using scRNA-seq profiling and genetic lineage tracing, we show that RUNX1+ PLCs are unaffected by androgen deprivation, and do not contribute to the regeneration of the distal luminal compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data showing that more than 90% of all RFP+ cells remained negative for NKX3.1 in all experimental arms (Figure 4I) and only modest increases in clone size after regeneration (Figure 4G).

claim: A transcriptionally similar RUNX1+ population emerges at the onset of embryonic prostate specification to populate the proximal region of the ducts.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that a transcriptionally similar RUNX1+ population emerges at the onset of embryonic prostate specification to populate the proximal region of the ducts.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq analysis of UGS explant cultures showing that the C2 cluster strongly resembles the adult Lum-D population (Figure 6I) and immunostaining data showing RUNX1 expression in the proximal region during development (Figure 5).

claim: RUNX1+ PLCs constitute an intrinsic castration-resistant and self-sustained lineage that emerges early during prostate development.
source: Collectively, our results reveal that RUNX1+ PLCs is an intrinsic castration-resistant and self-sustained lineage that emerges early during prostate development and provide new insights into the lineage relationships of the prostate epithelium.
evidence: This claim integrates multiple lines of evidence including castration resistance (Figure 4E), lack of contribution to distal regeneration (Figure 4I), and developmental emergence (Figures 5-7).

claim: Prostate development starts during embryogenesis at embryonic day (E) 15.5–16.5 with the emergence of the first prostatic buds from the rostral end of the urogenital sinus (UGS).
source: In mice, prostate development starts during embryogenesis at embryonic day (E) 15.5–16.5 with the emergence of the first prostatic buds from the rostral end of the urogenital sinus (UGS) (Bhatia-Gaur et al., 1999; Georgas et al., 2015; Keil et al., 2012; Toivanen and Shen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bhatia-Gaur et al., 1999; Georgas et al., 2015; Keil et al., 2012; Toivanen and Shen, 2017).

claim: The initial prostatic buds grow into the surrounding mesenchyme to develop postnatally and through puberty into a branched ductal network organized in distinct pairs of lobes, known as the anterior prostate (AP), dorsolateral prostate (DLP), and ventral prostate (VP).
source: These initial buds grow into the surrounding mesenchyme to develop postnatally and through puberty into a branched ductal network organized in distinct pairs of lobes, known as the anterior prostate (AP), dorsolateral prostate (DLP), and ventral prostate (VP) (Sugimura et al., 1986a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Sugimura et al., 1986a).

claim: The differentiated epithelium of the adult prostate gland is mainly composed of basal and luminal cells, interspersed with rare neuroendocrine cells.
source: The differentiated epithelium of the adult prostate gland is mainly composed of basal and luminal cells, interspersed with rare neuroendocrine cells (Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010; Toivanen and Shen, 2017; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010; Toivanen and Shen, 2017; Wang et al., 2001).

claim: Luminal cells form a layer of polarized tall columnar cells that depend on androgen signaling and produce the prostatic secretions.
source: Luminal cells form a layer of polarized tall columnar cells that depend on androgen signaling and produce the prostatic secretions.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about prostate luminal cell function.

claim: Basal cells act as a supportive layer located between the luminal cells and the surrounding stroma.
source: Basal cells act as a supportive layer located between the luminal cells and the surrounding stroma.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about prostate basal cell location and function.

claim: RUNX1 and NKX3.1 have a largely mutually exclusive expression pattern, with a sharp transition from RUNX1+ NKX3.1- to RUNX1- NKX3.1+ cells in the proximal region.
source: Using quantitative image-based cytometry (QBIC), we found that RUNX1 and NKX3.1 had a largely mutually exclusive expression pattern, with a sharp transition from RUNX1+ NKX3.1- to RUNX1- NKX3.1+ cells in the proximal region (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by QBIC analysis shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Proximal luminal cells have a compact organization, intense nuclear hematoxylin staining, and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
source: These proximal luminal cells had a unique histological profile, with a compact organization, intense nuclear hematoxylin staining, and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Distal luminal cells have a large cytoplasm with intense pink eosin staining, likely reflecting their secretory function.
source: In contrast, distal luminal cells had a large cytoplasm with intense pink eosin staining, likely reflecting their secretory function.
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, with the functional interpretation being speculative.

claim: Runx1 expression in the prostate is exclusively mediated by the proximal P2 promoter.
source: We found that Runx1 expression in the prostate was exclusively mediated by the proximal P2 promoter, in up to 30% of all epithelial EPCAM+ prostate cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: P2-Runx1:RFP is enriched in both basal (EPCAM+ CD49fhigh) and luminal (EPCAM+ CD24high) lineages of the proximal compared to the distal prostate.
source: Flow-cytometry profiling confirmed the enrichment of P2-Runx1:RFP in both basal (EPCAM+ CD49fhigh) and luminal (EPCAM+ CD24high) lineages of the proximal compared to the distal prostate (Figure 1C,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Basal cells are more efficient at forming organoids compared to all luminal fractions.
source: In line with previous reports, basal cells were more efficient at forming organoids compared to all luminal fractions (Drost et al., 2016, Kwon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation data in Figure 1F and citations to previous literature (Drost et al., 2016, Kwon et al., 2016).

claim: Proximal RFP+ luminal cells of the AP consistently display higher Organoid Formation Capacity (OFC) than the RFP- fraction.
source: Importantly, in the luminal fraction, proximal RFP+ luminal cells of the AP consistently displayed higher Organoid Formation Capacity (OFC) than the RFP- fraction (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Luminal RFP+ sorted cells of the DLP and VP have a greater OFC than RFP- cells.
source: Luminal RFP+ sorted cells of the DLP and VP also had a greater OFC than RFP- cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: AP proximal luminal RFP+-derived organoids are predominantly small unipotent K8+.
source: Interestingly, AP proximal luminal RFP+-derived organoids were predominantly small unipotent K8+, while the remainder fraction mainly gave larger unipotent K5+ organoids (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-mount immunostaining data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D–E.

claim: RUNX1+ PLCs have a particular predisposition to form unipotent K8+ hollow organoids.
source: RUNX1+ PLCs have a particular predisposition to form unipotent K8+ hollow organoids, suggesting a lineage bias toward the luminal identity, and highlighting differences within the luminal compartment of proximal and distal regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid morphology and lineage marker data shown in Figure 1G,H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: While intact prostates contained 22.8 ± 6.0% RFP+ epithelial cells, their frequency increased to 87 ± 6.0% following castration.
source: While intact prostates contained 22.8 ± 6.0% RFP+ epithelial cells, their frequency increased to 87 ± 6.0% following castration (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: High RUNX1 levels are no longer restricted to the proximal region after castration, and RFP is detected in virtually all basal cells of the AP, DLP, and VP, as well as more than 75% of the luminal castration-resistant cells.
source: High RUNX1 levels were no longer restricted to the proximal region, and RFP was detected in virtually all basal cells of the AP, DLP, and VP, as well as more than 75% of the luminal castration-resistant cells (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RUNX1-expressing cells often co-express TROP2 in castrated prostate epithelium.
source: RUNX1-expressing cells often co-expressed TROP2 (Figure 2E), known to be widely expressed in castrated prostate epithelium (Goldstein et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E and citations to previous literature (Goldstein et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2007).

claim: Only occasional RUNX1+ NKX3.1+ luminal cells are found in the distal regions of the castrated prostate.
source: Accordingly, we observed low, but detectable, levels of NKX3.1 in some luminal cells, but only occasional RUNX1+ NKX3.1+ luminal cells in the distal regions of the castrated prostate (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The clear transition from RUNX1+ to NKX3.1+ cells identified in the proximal luminal layer of intact mice is conserved after castration.
source: Importantly, the clear transition from RUNX1+ to NKX3.1+ cells identified in the proximal luminal layer of intact mice was conserved after castration (Figure 2D,ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D,ii.

claim: A total of 3825 prostate epithelial cells were retrieved from all sorted populations, with a median of 2846 genes per cell.
source: We retrieved a total of 3825 prostate epithelial cells from all sorted populations, with a median of 2846 genes per cell (see Materials and methods; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq quality control metrics described in Materials and methods and shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2A–G.

claim: Nine in silico computed clusters expressing canonical epithelial, basal, and luminal markers were identified.
source: We identified nine in silico computed clusters expressing canonical epithelial, basal, and luminal markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq clustering analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H–J.

claim: A large population of basal cells was annotated by merging three tightly connected subclusters broadly expressing Krt5, Krt14, and Trp63.
source: A large population of basal cells was annotated by merging three tightly connected subclusters broadly expressing Krt5, Krt14, and Trp63 (Figure 3B–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq clustering and gene expression data shown in Figure 3B–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,J.

claim: Luminal populations express surprisingly heterogeneous levels of canonical luminal markers such as Cd26/Dpp4, Cd24a, Krt8, and Krt18.
source: Luminal populations expressed surprisingly heterogeneous levels of canonical luminal markers such as Cd26/Dpp4, Cd24a, Krt8, and Krt18 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Lum-A/B/C/D are largely enriched in luminal cells originating from intact prostates, whereas Lum-E/F contain mainly castrated luminal cells.
source: Lum-A/B/C/D were largely enriched in luminal cells originating from intact prostates, whereas Lum-E/F contained mainly castrated luminal cells (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing cluster composition by treatment shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Lum-A/C/F mainly contain VP cells, while Lum-B/D/E have a majority of AP and DLP cells.
source: Interestingly, Lum-A/C/F mainly contained VP cells, while Lum-B/D/E had a majority of AP and DLP cells, indicating that the lobular identity of luminal cells in the intact prostate is conserved following castration (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing cluster composition by lobe shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The lobular identity of luminal cells in the intact prostate is conserved following castration.
source: Interestingly, Lum-A/C/F mainly contained VP cells, while Lum-B/D/E had a majority of AP and DLP cells, indicating that the lobular identity of luminal cells in the intact prostate is conserved following castration (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that lobe-specific clustering patterns are maintained between intact and castrated states, as shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Castrated basal cells are minimally affected by androgen-deprivation and cluster together with intact basal cells.
source: In contrast to luminal cells, castrated basal cells were minimally affected by androgen-deprivation and clustered together with intact basal cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq clustering data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Lum-D cluster predominantly consists of AP-derived RFP+ cells, as well as a small number of RFP+ DLP and VP cells.
source: The Lum-D cluster predominantly consisted of AP-derived RFP+ cells, as well as a small number of RFP+ DLP and VP cells (Figure 3F,H; Figure 3—figure supplements 2E, 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing cluster composition by lobe and RFP status shown in Figure 3F,H and Figure 3—figure supplements 2E, 3B and C.

claim: High Runx1 expression in Lum-D correlates with higher levels of Tacstd2/Trop2, Ly6 family members as well as Runx2.
source: High Runx1 expression in Lum-D correlated with higher levels of Tacstd2/Trop2, Ly6 family members as well as Runx2 (Figure 3D,G; Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 3D,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: Runx1 is barely detected in clusters Lum-B/C which express high levels of Nkx3-1.
source: In contrast, Runx1 was barely detected in clusters Lum-B/C which expressed high levels of Nkx3-1 while Lum-A cells expressed low levels of both Runx1 and Nkx3-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 3D,G.

claim: The Lum-D cluster is enriched in terms related to epithelial developmental processes, similar to Lum-E/F.
source: In contrast, the Lum-D cluster was enriched in terms related to epithelial developmental processes, similar to Lum-E/F (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–I.

claim: Partition-based graph abstraction uncovered a strong degree of connectivity between the mainly intact Lum-D and castrated Lum-E population.
source: This was supported by partition-based graph abstraction (Wolf et al., 2019), which uncovered a strong degree of connectivity between the mainly intact Lum-D and castrated Lum-E population (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PAGA analysis shown in Figure 3B and citation to the method (Wolf et al., 2019).

claim: The Lum-D cluster contains a small, but defined, subpopulation of castrated epithelial cells.
source: Additionally, the Lum-D cluster contained a small, but defined, subpopulation of castrated epithelial cells, suggesting the preservation of its identity upon androgen deprivation (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing cluster composition by treatment shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Very few genes (n = 103) are significantly differentially expressed between intact and castrated cells in the Lum-D cluster.
source: In this population, we found very few genes significantly differentially expressed between intact and castrated cells (n = 103; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis with results provided in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Androgen-regulated genes including Psca and Tspan1 are downregulated in the castrated subset of Lum-D, while strong contributors of the Lum-D identity such as Tacstd2/Trop2, Krt4 and Runx1 do not vary.
source: As expected, androgen-regulated genes including Psca and Tspan1 were downregulated in the castrated subset, while strong contributors of the Lum-D identity such as Tacstd2/Trop2, Krt4 and Runx1 did not vary (Figure 3—figure supplement 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4J.

claim: An average of 4.70 ± 2.8% prostate epithelial Runx1-expressing cells were genetically labeled with RFP upon tamoxifen injection.
source: Using this model, we could genetically label an average of 4.70 ± 2.8% prostate epithelial Runx1-expressing cells with RFP upon tamoxifen injection (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority of labeled cells are located in the proximal region of the prostate.
source: Consistent with the expression pattern of Runx1, the majority of labeled cells were located in the proximal region of the prostate (Figure 4C), and co-expressed Keratin 4 (K4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E), previously found enriched in Lum-D cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The absolute number of RFP+ marked cells remains stable following surgical castration.
source: Following surgical castration, we found that the absolute number of RFP+ marked cells remained stable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The frequency of RFP+ cells in the epithelial compartment increases by ~4.3 fold after castration.
source: However, the frequency of RFP+ cells in the epithelial compartment increased by ~4.3 fold (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) indicating that Runx1-expressing cells have an enhanced capacity to survive castration compared to Runx1-negative cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Runx1-expressing cells have an enhanced capacity to survive castration compared to Runx1-negative cells.
source: However, the frequency of RFP+ cells in the epithelial compartment increased by ~4.3 fold (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) indicating that Runx1-expressing cells have an enhanced capacity to survive castration compared to Runx1-negative cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that RFP+ cell frequency increases while absolute numbers remain stable, indicating preferential survival.

claim: Only 0.71 ± 0.2‰ RFP+ epithelial cells are found in the regenerated prostate, which is comparable to the intact state.
source: Surprisingly, only 0.71 ± 0.2‰ RFP+ epithelial cells were found in the regenerated prostate, which was comparable to the intact state (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: There is a minor ~2-fold increase in the frequency of larger clones (2–4 cells) after regeneration.
source: Although the majority of RFP+ clones consisted of single cells, we did observe a minor ~2-fold increase in the frequency of larger clones (2–4 cells) after regeneration, highlighting a modest contribution of RFP labeled cells during prostate regeneration (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by clone size quantification data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: Most RFP marked cells are luminal K8+ in intact, castrated, and regenerated prostates.
source: We found that most RFP marked cells were luminal K8+ in intact, castrated, and regenerated prostates (Figure 4F,H), with only a few basal K5+ RFP+ cells detected in distal areas (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4F,H.

claim: More than 90% of all RFP+ cells remain negative for NKX3.1 in all experimental arms.
source: Strikingly, more than 90% of all RFP+ cells remained negative for NKX3.1 in all experimental arms (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: At E18.5, RUNX1 is mainly found in the K8high inner layers of the stratified urogenital epithelium (UGE).
source: At E18.5, once the first prostate buds have emerged, RUNX1 was mainly found in the K8high inner layers of the stratified urogenital epithelium (UGE) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RUNX1+ cells at E18.5 co-express K4 and LY6D.
source: Interestingly, these cells also co-expressed K4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), previously found in the Lum D population (Figure 3D), as well as LY6D, recently shown to mark a subset of adult luminal progenitors (Barros-Silva et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B and citations to previous work (Barros-Silva et al., 2018).

claim: RUNX1 expression is low in p63+ and K5+ cells at E18.5.
source: In contrast, RUNX1 expression was low in p63+ and K5+ cells, either lining the outer UGE or found in the tips of premature NKX3.1+ prostate buds (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: At postnatal day 14 (P14), RUNX1 is broadly expressed in the proximal region, mainly in K4+ luminal cells and in some K5+ or p63+ cells.
source: At postnatal day 14 (P14), a prepubescent stage when most of the initial branching events have already occurred (Sugimura et al., 1986a; Tika et al., 2019), RUNX1 was broadly expressed in the proximal region (Figure 5D), mainly in K4+ luminal cells and in some K5+ or p63+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E, and citations to previous work (Sugimura et al., 1986a; Tika et al., 2019).

claim: NKX3.1+ cells at P14 are found in distal locations, largely distinct from RUNX1+ cells.
source: Conversely, NKX3.1+ cells were found in distal locations, largely distinct from RUNX1+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: On day 0 (E15.5) of UGS explant culture, RUNX1 is detected at the rostral end of the UGE, particularly within the inner layers of the stratified epithelium.
source: On day 0 (E15.5), RUNX1 was detected at the rostral end of the UGE, particularly within the inner layers of the stratified epithelium.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: After 1 day in UGS explant culture, NKX3.1 expression emerges in RUNX1+ cells located in the outer layers of the UGE.
source: After 1 day in culture, NKX3.1 expression emerged in RUNX1+ cells located in the outer layers of the UGE, while defined budding was yet to be observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: On day 2 of UGS explant culture, NKX3.1+ prostate buds are evident and have reduced or absent RUNX1 expression.
source: On day 2, NKX3.1+ prostate buds were evident and had reduced or absent RUNX1 expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In mature UGS explants, distal tips are mainly NKX3.1+, whereas the proximal area remains RUNX1+.
source: This pattern was conserved in the mature explant, in which distal tips were mainly NKX3.1+, whereas the proximal area remained RUNX1+ (Figure 5G,H), and co-expressed LY6D and K4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and QBIC data shown in Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Cellular proliferation marked by Ki67 is more substantial in distal regions of UGS explants.
source: Cellular proliferation marked by Ki67 was more substantial in distal regions, suggesting that most of the expansion did not take place in the RUNX1+ compartment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ki67 immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: After data processing of UGS explant scRNA-seq, 3937 developing prostatic cells were retained, with a median of 3608 genes per cell.
source: After data processing, 3937 developing prostatic cells were retained, with a median of 3608 genes per cell (see Materials and methods; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq quality control metrics described in Materials and methods and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cellular populations in UGS explant cultures were divided into nine clusters, annotated C0 to C8.
source: Cellular populations were divided into nine clusters, annotated C0 to C8 (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq clustering analysis shown in Figure 6C–E.

claim: C0/C1 contain the majority of D0 and D1 derived cells, while C2-C8 emerge and expand at later time points.
source: C0/C1 contained the majority of D0 and D1 derived cells, while C2-C8 emerged and expanded at later time points.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing cluster composition by time point shown in Figure 6B,E.

claim: C4-C6 have a more pronounced 'basal' identity compared to the other clusters in UGS explants.
source: Nevertheless, C4-C6 had a more pronounced 'basal' identity compared to the other clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Runx1 is highly expressed in clusters having lower Nkx3-1 levels, including C0, C1, C2, and C4.
source: Consistent with our previous results, Runx1 was highly expressed in clusters having lower Nkx3-1 levels, including C0, C1, C2, and C4 (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The 'Lum-D' derived signature is highly enriched in C2 compared to all the other adult luminal population signatures.
source: Strikingly, the 'Lum-D' derived signature was highly enriched in C2 compared to all the other adult luminal population signatures, suggesting that the 'Lum-D' fate is determined early during prostate development.
evidence: This claim is supported by AUCell signature enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: The 'Lum-D' fate is determined early during prostate development.
source: Strikingly, the 'Lum-D' derived signature was highly enriched in C2 compared to all the other adult luminal population signatures, suggesting that the 'Lum-D' fate is determined early during prostate development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the C2 cluster in early development shares strong transcriptional similarity with the adult Lum-D population.

claim: The singular identity of C2 is characterized by genes previously found highly expressed in the adult 'Lum-D' population, including Tacstd2/Trop2, Krt4, Psca, as well as Ly6d and Nupr1.
source: The singular identity of C2 was characterized by genes previously found highly expressed in the adult 'Lum-D' population, including Tacstd2/Trop2, Krt4, Psca, as well as Ly6d and Nupr1 (Figure 6H; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The majority of RFP labeled cells in UGS explant lineage tracing are in the most proximal RUNX1+ subset and rarely found in the distal area of the branches.
source: The majority of the RFP labeled cells were in the most proximal RUNX1+ subset and rarely found in the distal area of the branches, where RUNX1- cells reside (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The proportion of RFP+ RUNX1+ cells remains stable between days 2 and 7 in UGS explant lineage tracing.
source: Accordingly, the proportion of RFP+ RUNX1+ cells remained stable between days 2 and 7 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The fraction of RFP+ cells co-expressing p63 remains unchanged throughout UGS explant culture.
source: Also, the fraction of RFP+ cells co-expressing p63 remained unchanged throughout the culture (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C), while a small fraction diversified into either K5+ or K8+ cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Runx1-expressing cells only marginally contribute to the expansion of the NKX3.1 compartment in UGS explants.
source: Overall, this indicates that Runx1-expressing cells only marginally contribute to the expansion of the NKX3.1 compartment (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data showing low percentages of RFP+ NKX3.1+ cells shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The fraction of K4+ RFP labeled cells increases from 56.9 ± 10.6% to 74.1 ± 3.0% between day 2 and 7 in UGS explant lineage tracing.
source: Interestingly, the fraction of K4+ RFP labeled cells increased from 56.9 ± 10.6% to 74.1 ± 3.0% between day 2 and 7 (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7F,G.

claim: There is an increase of RFP+ cells expressing Nupr1 between day 2 and 7 in UGS explant lineage tracing.
source: There was also an increase of RFP+ cells expressing Nupr1, another marker of the C2 cluster (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: Only a small subset of Runx1-expressing cells contributes to the expansion of NKX3.1+ lineage, found in the distal region of the developing prostatic buds.
source: Taken together, these results show that only a small subset of Runx1-expressing cells contributes to the expansion of NKX3.1+ lineage, found in the distal region of the developing prostatic buds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from lineage tracing data showing low contribution to NKX3.1+ cells (Figure 7E-G).

claim: The majority of Runx1-expressing cells preferentially remain in the proximal region of the premature buds, where the proximal luminal lineage is established.
source: Instead, the majority of Runx1-expressing cells preferentially remain in the proximal region of the premature buds, where the proximal luminal lineage is established.
evidence: This claim is inferred from lineage tracing data showing enrichment of RFP+ cells in proximal regions and increased K4 expression (Figure 7).

claim: RUNX1 is increasingly implicated in hormone-associated epithelia including breast, uterine, ovarian, and prostate cancers.
source: Interestingly, increasing evidence implicates RUNX1 in the biology and pathology of hormone-associated epithelia (Lie-A-Ling et al., 2020; Riggio and Blyth, 2017; Scheitz and Tumbar, 2013), including breast (Browne et al., 2015; Chimge et al., 2016; Ferrari et al., 2014; van Bragt et al., 2014), uterine (Planagumà et al., 2004; Planagumà et al., 2006), ovarian (Keita et al., 2013), and prostate cancers (Banach-Petrosky et al., 2007; Scheitz et al., 2012; Takayama et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: RUNX transcription factors are master regulators of lineage commitment and cell fate.
source: RUNX transcription factors (TF) are master regulators of lineage commitment and cell fate (Mevel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Mevel et al., 2019).

claim: RUNX1 is essential for the ontogeny of the hematopoietic system.
source: In particular, RUNX1 is essential for the ontogeny of the hematopoietic system and alterations of RUNX1 have been associated with a broad spectrum of hematological malignancies.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about RUNX1 function in hematopoiesis.

claim: Alterations of RUNX1 have been associated with a broad spectrum of hematological malignancies.
source: In particular, RUNX1 is essential for the ontogeny of the hematopoietic system and alterations of RUNX1 have been associated with a broad spectrum of hematological malignancies.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about RUNX1 in cancer.

claim: Surgical castration-induced prostate involution has proven an invaluable tool to identify progenitor castration-resistant cell populations.
source: In mice, surgical castration-induced prostate involution has proven an invaluable tool to identify progenitor castration-resistant cell populations, characterized by their ability to survive in the absence of androgens, and to fully regenerate an intact adult prostate after re-administration of testosterone (Barros-Silva et al., 2018; Kwon et al., 2016; McAuley et al., 2019; Tsujimura et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Yoo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Castration-resistant cell populations are characterized by their ability to survive in the absence of androgens, and to fully regenerate an intact adult prostate after re-administration of testosterone.
source: In mice, surgical castration-induced prostate involution has proven an invaluable tool to identify progenitor castration-resistant cell populations, characterized by their ability to survive in the absence of androgens, and to fully regenerate an intact adult prostate after re-administration of testosterone (Barros-Silva et al., 2018; Kwon et al., 2016; McAuley et al., 2019; Tsujimura et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009; Yoo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature defining castration-resistant cells.

claim: Several studies have proposed that progenitor populations with distinct physiological roles and regenerative capacity reside at different locations within the prostate.
source: In addition, several studies have proposed that progenitor populations with distinct physiological roles and regenerative capacity reside at different locations within the prostate (Burger et al., 2005; Crowell et al., 2019; Goldstein et al., 2008; Goto et al., 2006; Kwon et al., 2016; Leong et al., 2008; McNeal, 1981; Tsujimura et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The precise cellular hierarchy and how it is established during development remains controversial.
source: However, the precise cellular hierarchy and how it is established during development remains controversial.
evidence: This claim represents a summary of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The prostate is mostly quiescent under homeostatic conditions.
source: Despite being mostly quiescent under homeostatic conditions, the prostate gland encompasses incredible plasticity.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about prostate homeostasis.

claim: The prostate gland encompasses incredible plasticity.
source: Despite being mostly quiescent under homeostatic conditions, the prostate gland encompasses incredible plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsequent discussion of regeneration and plasticity experiments.

claim: Runx1 expression is controlled by two promoters, P1 and P2, that respectively drive the expression of the Runx1c and the Runx1b isoform.
source: Runx1 expression is controlled by two promoters, P1 and P2, that respectively drive the expression of the Runx1c and the Runx1b isoform (Mevel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Mevel et al., 2019).

claim: The Lum-D cluster corresponds to the distinct RUNX1+ luminal cells identified in the proximal region of all three prostate lobes.
source: These results suggest that the Lum-D cluster corresponds to the distinct RUNX1+ luminal cells identified in the proximal region of all three prostate lobes (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between Runx1 expression in the Lum-D cluster and the spatial localization of RUNX1+ cells.

claim: The Lum-D population corresponds to PLCs.
source: These results suggest that the Lum-D cluster corresponds to the distinct RUNX1+ luminal cells identified in the proximal region of all three prostate lobes (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the spatial and molecular characteristics of the Lum-D cluster matching those of PLCs.

claim: The Lum-D population may contain intrinsically castration-resistant luminal cells.
source: The tight transcriptional relationship observed between high Runx1 expressing clusters Lum-D and Lum-E/F suggest that the Lum-D population, which corresponds to PLCs, may contain intrinsically castration-resistant luminal cells.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the transcriptional similarity between Lum-D and castration-enriched Lum-E/F clusters.

claim: RFP+ cells, including PLCs, are mostly unaffected by fluctuations in androgen levels during regression-regeneration assays.
source: Thus, these results indicate that RFP+ cells, including PLCs, are mostly unaffected by fluctuations in androgen levels during regression-regeneration assays.
evidence: This claim is inferred from lineage tracing data showing stable RFP+ cell numbers and phenotypes across experimental conditions.

claim: RUNX1 expression marks intrinsically castration-resistant luminal cells that do not contribute substantially to the expansion of luminal NKX3.1+ cells during prostate regeneration.
source: RUNX1 expression marks intrinsically castration-resistant luminal cells that do not contribute substantially to the expansion of luminal NKX3.1+ cells during prostate regeneration.
evidence: This claim integrates lineage tracing data showing castration resistance and lack of contribution to NKX3.1+ regeneration.

claim: RUNX1 and NKX3.1 already mark distinct cellular lineages during embryonic prostate organogenesis.
source: The specific spatial expression pattern of RUNX1 in proximal luminal cells, largely mutually exclusive with NKX3.1, suggests that these two transcription factors already mark distinct cellular lineages during embryonic prostate organogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutually exclusive expression patterns observed during development.

claim: Prostate budding originates from a subset of cells located in the outer layers of the stratified UGE, transiently marked by RUNX1 and NKX3.1.
source: These results suggest that prostate budding originates from a subset of cells located in the outer layers of the stratified UGE, transiently marked by RUNX1 and NKX3.1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from immunostaining data showing co-expression of RUNX1 and NKX3.1 in outer UGE layers at day 1 of explant culture.

claim: During embryonic prostate development, Runx1 expression is already primarily confined to the proximal region of the prostatic ducts, in a distinct compartment from NKX3.1+ cells.
source: During embryonic prostate development, Runx1 expression is already primarily confined to the proximal region of the prostatic ducts, in a distinct compartment from NKX3.1+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data from UGS explant cultures showing spatial segregation of RUNX1 and NKX3.1 expression.

claim: Adult 'Lum-D'/PLCs share strong similarities with the unique C2 population identified in embryonic explant cultures.
source: Collectively, our scRNA-seq analysis show that adult 'Lum-D'/PLCs share strong similarities with the unique C2 population identified in embryonic explant cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene signature enrichment analysis showing high similarity between C2 and Lum-D populations.

claim: The distinct proximal luminal lineage is established at the very onset of prostate specification.
source: This suggests that the distinct proximal luminal lineage is established at the very onset of prostate specification.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the C2 cluster emerges early in development and shares characteristics with adult PLCs.

claim: Runx1-expressing cells preferentially populate the emerging proximal luminal identity during development.
source: Subsequent lineage-tracing experiments indicated that Runx1-expressing cells preferentially populate the emerging proximal luminal identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data showing enrichment of RFP+ cells in proximal regions and increased K4 expression over time.

claim: Basal and luminal lineages have previously been shown to be largely self-sustained using generic basal and luminal Cre drivers.
source: Basal and luminal lineages have previously been shown to be largely self-sustained using generic basal and luminal Cre drivers (Choi et al., 2012; Ousset et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Choi et al., 2012; Ousset et al., 2012).

claim: Whether distinct subpopulations of luminal cells contribute to the regeneration of the others remains poorly understood.
source: However, whether distinct subpopulations of luminal cells contribute to the regeneration of the others remains poorly understood (Wang et al., 2009; Yoo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim represents a summary of the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The model of self-sustained basal and luminal populations might be extended to individual luminal subpopulations.
source: Thus, we suggest that the model of self-sustained basal and luminal populations might be extended to individual luminal subpopulations.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that RUNX1+ PLCs are self-sustained.

claim: Pten loss induced in Psca-expressing cells of the proximal prostate can initiate prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia.
source: Along these lines, recent work by Guo and colleagues indicates that Pten loss induced in Psca-expressing cells of the proximal prostate can initiate prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Guo et al., 2020).

claim: The emerging C2/Lum-D population retains a more embryonic-like program, which may relate to their intrinsic castration-resistant potential.
source: Finally, our study suggests that the emerging C2/Lum-D population retains a more embryonic-like program, which may relate to their intrinsic castration-resistant potential and have broader relevance to cancer treatment.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the transcriptional similarity between developmental and adult populations and their castration resistance.

claim: This study constitutes the first comprehensive single-cell atlas covering both intact and castrated adult mouse prostates, annotated by their lobe of origin.
source: To our knowledge, this constitutes the first comprehensive single-cell atlas covering both intact and castrated adult mouse prostates, annotated by their lobe of origin.
evidence: This claim represents a statement about the novelty of the dataset presented in this study.

claim: The adult scRNA-seq dataset highlighted an extensive degree of cellular heterogeneity, in particular within the luminal epithelia.
source: In particular, our adult scRNA-seq dataset highlighted an extensive degree of cellular heterogeneity, in particular within the luminal epithelia.
evidence: This claim is supported by the identification of multiple luminal clusters (Lum-A through Lum-F) with distinct gene expression profiles.

claim: The Lum-D subset appears to be the equivalent of the 'L2' or 'LumP', or 'Lum-C' clusters identified in recent studies.
source: Of note, this subset appears to be the equivalent of the 'L2' (Karthaus et al., 2020) or 'LumP' (Crowley et al., 2020), or 'Lum-C' (Guo et al., 2020) clusters identified in recent studies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison with other published datasets, supported by citations.

claim: RUNX1+ PLCs exhibit a greater organoid forming potential compared to the remaining luminal fraction, consistent with previous reports isolating similar proximal populations using different markers such as SCA-1, TROP2 or CD26.
source: We demonstrate that these RUNX1+ PLCs exhibit a greater organoid forming potential compared to the remaining luminal fraction, consistent with previous reports isolating similar proximal populations using different markers such as SCA-1, TROP2 or CD26 (Crowley et al., 2020; Goldstein et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid formation data and citations to previous literature.

claim: The greater clonogenicity of RUNX1+ PLCs may be linked to the gene expression profile of the corresponding Lum-D population, suggesting a more immature epithelial state, committed to the luminal lineage but not the secretory function of the prostate.
source: The greater clonogenicity of RUNX1+ PLCs may in fact be linked to the gene expression profile of the corresponding Lum-D population, suggesting a more immature epithelial state, committed to the luminal lineage but not the secretory function of the prostate.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on gene ontology analysis showing developmental rather than secretory functions in Lum-D.

claim: RUNX1+ PLCs may act as a latent niche of 'facultative' luminal stem cells, primed to generate a structured prostatic epithelium under defined conditions.
source: Similar to the enhanced regenerative potential of glandular basal cells under specific regenerative conditions (Centonze et al., 2020), it is tempting to speculate that these cells act as a latent niche of 'facultative' luminal stem cells (Clevers and Watt, 2018), primed to generate a structured prostatic epithelium under defined conditions.
evidence: This claim is speculative, drawing an analogy to other stem cell systems and supported by citations.

claim: The scRNA-seq of the developing prostate revealed a broad basal identity, supporting the presence of multipotent basal progenitors during embryonic development.
source: Our scRNA-seq of the developing prostate revealed a broad basal identity, supporting the presence of multipotent basal progenitors during embryonic development (Ousset et al., 2012; Pignon et al., 2013), switching to unipotency postnatally (Tika et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Multipotent basal progenitors switch to unipotency postnatally.
source: Our scRNA-seq of the developing prostate revealed a broad basal identity, supporting the presence of multipotent basal progenitors during embryonic development (Ousset et al., 2012; Pignon et al., 2013), switching to unipotency postnatally (Tika et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Tika et al., 2019).

claim: Prostate epithelial regeneration is driven by almost all luminal cells persisting in castrated prostates.
source: Recently, it was proposed that prostate epithelial regeneration is driven by almost all luminal cells persisting in castrated prostates (Karthaus et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Karthaus et al., 2020).

claim: Not all luminal subsets retain the same in vivo regenerative potential in response to androgen stimulation.
source: Our results are compatible with this model, but we further demonstrate that not all luminal subsets retain the same in vivo regenerative potential in response to androgen stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data showing differential regenerative contributions of RUNX1+ versus RUNX1- luminal cells.
